1:
Calvin sets the vision in its occasion. Zechariah was sent to encourage weak minds, since hope was difficult in the midst of so much confusion: only a small part of the nation had returned, enemies at once arose to hinder the building of city and temple, and the faithful, looking at their circumstances, could hardly entertain any hope of the redemption promised them. So the prophet labours throughout to show that they must look for more than the aspect of things gave them reason to expect, and direct their eyes to a power of God not yet manifested, which God purposely withheld in order to try their patience. Clarke gives the same setting historically, that while the Jews were rebuilding their adversaries endeavoured to stop the work, so that the vision assures them God would not give up a people plucked as brands out of the fire.

Whether Joshua is seen as himself or as a figure divides them. Gill sets out the personal case first, that he had come up out of the captivity, was principally concerned in the building, had many enemies, and had fallen into sin, or his sons had in marrying foreign wives, so that Satan was ready to accuse him; but Gill judges it better to take him not personally but typically, as representing the state of the priesthood under the second temple, or the church itself. Ellicott states the representative reading plainly, that in the guilt as in the pardon and the promise Joshua stood for the people,. Henry keeps both together, observing that the prophet must often have seen the high priest and known him well, but saw only how he appeared before men, so that to learn how he stood before the Lord he had to be shown it in vision — men being really as they are with God and not as they appear in the eye of the world.

Henry also draws out the name. There was a Joshua principally concerned in the first settling of Israel in the land, and here is another of the same name active in their second settlement after the captivity; the name is the same as Jesus and signifies Saviour, and both men were figures of the one who was to come, our chief captain and our chief priest. Ellicott traces the philology of it at length as the name of the Saviour of the world, following the oldest form through its contractions into the shorter Hebrew forms and thence into the Greek that yields Jesus.

Who the angel of the Lord is draws a range of answers. Wesley says simply Christ, and Gill identifies the speaker with the Angel of the Lord who is here called Jehovah, being the Son of God and properly God. Henry likewise makes him Christ, the Lord of the angels, to whom even the high priests of Aaron's order were accountable. Keil and Delitzsch treat the identification more warily. They render the rebuke as spoken by Jehovah, that is by the angel of Jehovah, but attach a caution about the use made of the formula in the epistle of Jude: the words Jehovah rebuke thee are a standing formula for uttering the threat of a divine judgment, from which no conclusion may be drawn about the relation of the persons, so that the angel is not to be placed beneath Jehovah on the strength of them. Clarke and Ellicott both notice the same connection with that epistle, Clarke paraphrasing the rebuke as a demand whether Satan would have destroyed those whom God has justified, and Ellicott adding that Satan is justly rebuked, since none shall lay anything to the charge of God's chosen. Of the fire, Ellicott says it is the penal suffering of the captivity.
3:
The filthy garments are read consistently as guilt, but with different reference. Gill reports the Jewish interpretation that the sin was that of Joshua's children in marrying foreign wives, or his own in doing so, and mentions a further suggestion that it was sloth in rebuilding the temple, adding that Satan had aggravated whatever it was. Clarke widens it from the man to the nation: the people were in a forlorn and destitute condition, and besides that they were sinful and the priesthood defiled, so that nothing but the mercy of God could save them. Ellicott keeps the ritual point, that such garments would render him unfit to appear before God as priest and are a symbol of the guilt and defilement of sin. Wesley calls them the emblem of a poor or sinful state.

Who does the stripping and clothing is more disputed than it looks. Wesley makes the speaker Christ and those addressed the ministerial angels, and draws the conclusion that what angels could not take away Christ did, removing the filth of sin with both its guilt and its stain. Ellicott reaches the same identification by usage rather than doctrine, noting that the phrase for those who stood before him means courtiers and counsellors and here probably denotes angels of a grade inferior to the angel of the Lord; and he takes the iniquity removed to be that of the priest and of the people whose representative he is. On the tense he differs from the received version, preferring and I clothe thee, which he classes as an aorist of the immediate past. Gill has the Angel of the Lord answering both the accusations of Satan and the entreaties of Joshua.

Ellicott alone explains why the prophet interrupts to ask for the mitre. He seems to have felt constrained to make the request from an idea that the changing of the raiment might signify only the removal of the high priest's own guilt, and the mitre matters because it was on the turban that the golden plate inscribed with holiness to the Lord was fastened. Wesley reads the interruption as boldness, the prophet desiring for Joshua what would add to his authority and asking it of Christ himself. Clarke takes the mitre as the sign that the office of the high priesthood, which had been defiled and profaned, was now renewed to him,. Gill hesitates over whose words they are, allowing that they may be the Father's, who has all the angels at his command and always regards the intercession of his Son. Ellicott adds only that the word rendered fair means clean.

On the charge that follows, Gill observes that the Angel not only gave his word but annexed his oath, calling heaven and earth to witness, in order to confirm Joshua's faith in the promises about to be made and in the blessings already bestowed. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same verses as a prophetic address in which the angel of the Lord expounds the symbolic re-clothing according to its typical significance for the continuance and the future of the kingdom of God. Clarke enlarges the conditions from the priest to the whole people, so that if Israel restored to their own land will walk in God's ways they shall be part of his family and have mansions in eternal glory with all them that are sanctified. Henry states the principle he finds governing the whole: all whom God calls to any office he finds fit or else makes so; and he adds that as the promises made to David often pass into promises of the Messiah, so the promises made here look forward to Christ, of whose priesthood this one was a shadow.
8:
Henry states the principle that governs the section: as the promises made to David slide insensibly into promises of the Messiah, whose kingdom David's was a type of, so the promises made to Joshua rise at once as far as Christ, whose priesthood Joshua's was a shadow of — not only in continuing the line of Aaron but especially in reviving the correspondence between heaven and earth that the captivity had interrupted. Christ is a high priest, as this one was, for sinners and sufferers, to mediate for those who have lain under guilt and wrath; and Henry adds a reason why the man himself needed to understand it, since all the virtue and usefulness of his own priesthood to the church depended on and was derived from the priesthood of Christ.

What the fellows are called is variously understood. Ellicott takes the phrase literally as men of sign, meaning men to whom signs are given and for whom miracles are wrought, and reports the alternative that it means persons accustomed to interpret the enigmatical sayings of prophets, with the Greek version rendering it men who observe portents. Clarke translates it figurative men, whose office and ministration prefigured Christ, and treats the promise of the Branch as following immediately from that. Wesley reads the wonder as other people's rather than a divine designation, the unbelieving Jews wondering at these men and at the labour and expense of attempting to build such a house. Ellicott adds a grammatical note on the change of person in the clause and prefers a plainer rendering of the particle that introduces the promise.

On the Branch there is one dissent to record and a general agreement. Gill takes it of the Messiah, the antitype of Joshua and of all the priests; Wesley says the Messiah likewise and adds that the Father will bring forth a work more wonderful still. Clarke reports that an archbishop understood it of Zerubbabel, as grandson of Jeconiah and heir to the throne of Judah, and notes that the Chaldee has my servant the Messiah; his own judgment is against the Zerubbabel reading.

The stone produces the sharpest division. Gill denies that it is the plummet or the foundation stone laid by Zerubbabel in the high priest's presence, and makes it Christ the stone of Israel whom the builders refused, laid before Joshua that he might build his faith upon it, take comfort from it and instruct others in the use of it. Clarke allows the allusion to the temple's foundation stone but insists the thing signified is Christ and none other, on whom the whole church rests as a building on its foundation. Wesley reads it as a particular stone pointed out, with the seven eyes so placed that they might look many ways, an emblem of Christ's perfect knowledge and wisdom, where Clarke supposes the eyes to mean the providence of God under which the work would be completed and suggests an allusion to the seven counsellors who attended the persons of the eastern kings. Ellicott objects on grammar. If the received sense were right, he argues, the following words ought to read upon that stone rather than upon one stone; the singular is a noun of multitude and means the stones, the material stones with which the house was to be built, so that laying them before Joshua figures the whole command to build, and the one stone is one particular stone among them. Of the closing verse, Gill takes the day for the whole gospel dispensation beginning with the incarnation, Clarke for a time of liberty in which each will invite and encourage another to believe, and Wesley for the day of removing the sins of the people, when men call one another to the sweet fruit of vine and fig tree and repose in tranquillity, quiet from the fear of evil.
